Preface to the Publication of Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light

The two phrases “mind-only Pure Land” and “self-nature Amitabha” are the crucial words by which the sages and worthies of old — those who thoroughly realized mind-only and perfectly manifested the self-nature — out of their great compassionate hearts strained to expound the teaching and urged people to penetrate deeply into mind-only and the self-nature. But since they bring up mind-only and the self-nature, why did they not speak of a mind-only Huazang or a self-nature Vairocana? Why did they not speak of a mind-only Vulture Peak or a self-nature Shakyamuni? Why did they not speak of a mind-only Tusita or a self-nature Maitreya? Why did they speak only of a mind-only Pure Land and a self-nature Amitabha? What is the reason? It is simply that mind-only is hard to realize and the self-nature hard to manifest. Now, if we would have them realized and manifested, we must rely on the Pure Land Dharma-gate, in which our World-Honored One Shakyamuni, out of a thorough compassion, unasked and speaking of himself, told the greatly wise Shariputra directly, causing people to hold fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha and to resolve to seek birth in the Western [Pure Land]. Then the wise above and the foolish below, monks and laity, men and women, every living being, each with this present fleeting thought, his karmic consciousness, takes as its single object the one phrase, the great name of Amitabha Buddha’s ten thousand virtues; and holding it long, he can cause ignorance and karmic consciousness gradually to melt away. Until they are melted away and utterly purified, through the six periods of day and night all is clear and distinct: there is only the one phrase, the great name of Amitabha Buddha’s ten thousand virtues, wholly appearing, standing alone and perfectly manifest. If he then seeks again for the arising-and-ceasing false mind of ignorance and karmic consciousness, it is utterly unobtainable. Moreover, apart from Amitabha’s great name there is no other self-nature; apart from the self-nature there is no other Amitabha. The self-nature is Amitabha; Amitabha belongs wholly to the self-nature. Amitabha and the self-nature are not two, not different; therefore it is called self-nature Amitabha. When the work of Buddha-recitation reaches this, the realm of Western Ultimate Bliss naturally and constantly appears before one. Whether in city or deep mountain, there is no hill or hollow, no filth or evil appearance. With eyes open or closed, one sees only gold for ground, pools of varied jewels, towers of the seven precious things, water of eight merits, four-colored lotus flowers, richly fragrant and radiant. Lifting the foot and setting it down, one adorns the Buddha-land. Outside the mind no land, outside the land no mind; mind and land are one suchness; therefore it is called mind-only Pure Land. The ancients, having with this personally verified the perfect and true realm, universally offered it to their fellows: fearing that people might suspect that reciting the Buddha and seeking birth in the West is to cast away the root and chase the branch, to seek outward, they therefore spoke of self-nature Amitabha and mind-only Pure Land. They wished everyone to recite together the Amitabha who welcomes and guides within the self-nature, and together to be born in the Ultimate Bliss Pure Land within mind-only, hoping that after birth in the West they might all thoroughly realize mind-only, perfectly manifest the self-nature, together perfect the all-embracing wisdom, and together verify bodhi. Their compassion was deep and earnest; no weightier earnestness could surpass it. People today, though their karmic hindrances are heavy and they lack the strength of the ancients, cannot personally realize it in this life. But if they can well apprehend the intent of the ancients and cultivate accordingly, each according to his capacity and strength, they too may return together to the Pure Land Dharma-gate, enter together the sea of Amitabha’s vows, and at the end of life leave the Saha world and be reborn in Ultimate Bliss — as surely as holding a tally in hand. This unwise one has recited the Buddha for more than twenty years and long heard these two phrases, yet always found them inexplicable. I see only that those who bring up these two phrases today are people of mere verbal liberation, who talk emptiness with every mouthful and walk existence with every step. When they see people reciting the Buddha and seeking birth in the Pure Land, they rebuke them outright: “Mind-only Pure Land — why seek a Western Pure Land? Self-nature Amitabha — why recite a Western Amitabha?” They take these two phrases as a powerful basis for demolishing others’ Buddha-recitation. As for how they came by this, it is nothing but having read a few volumes of recorded sayings in the texts and heard a few koans from the side of a teacher. Seeing such phrases as “Bodhi has no tree, the bright mirror has no stand; originally not a single thing, where could dust alight?”, “the three realms are mind-only, the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only,” “mind-only Pure Land, self-nature Amitabha,” they then take their own false mind of karmic consciousness to be mind-only and the self-nature. Beyond this false mind of karmic consciousness they do not understand fact and principle, are unversed in the provisional and the real, and merely trust to empty words while discarding cultivation. They think that just as one is, here and now, is the thing itself — why bother to cultivate otherwise? Pitiable: a muddled suchness, a woolly Buddha-nature. They slander the great prajna, ruining themselves and misleading others. They forever wipe out completely all the good dharmas contained in their own real mind of original awakening, and let all evil dharmas remain in the mind. Thus life after life they sink in the sea of suffering with no way out. Those whom the Tathagata calls pitiable are precisely such people. I shall now make a simile to prove the error of such people who do not know mind-only and the self-nature.

What is the simile? Mind-only and the self-nature may be likened to the substance of fine, firm, precious true gold. Having this substance of true gold, it can of course produce all kinds of functions that follow marks and establish names. Suppose, for example, that a man of purity uses true gold [substance] to make a pure vase [mark], fills it with clean, bright, pure water, offers it before the Buddha day after day, and constantly guards and wipes it [function]: this may be called a true-gold pure vase [here name and reality accord, signifying that what the ancients pointed to as mind-only Pure Land and self-nature Amitabha must surely lead people to recite the Buddha in earnest until they thoroughly realize and perfectly manifest it]. Suppose again that a wasteful rich man, his heart cherishing nothing, uses true gold [substance] to make a chamber pot or a bedpan [mark], and uses it all day long to hold urine and excrement [function]. It holds only brimming filth and urine, and no one ever wipes or washes it, but lets it stink unbearably: this should be called a true-gold chamber pot, or a true-gold bedpan [in the three objects above, though the gold substance is the same, mark and function are wholly different]. Suppose there appears a man who does not know fragrance from stench, purity from filth, and knows nothing at all of the respective marks and functions of a pure vase, a chamber pot, or a bedpan. He only hears people say that there is a true-gold pure vase, and does not know what mark and function a pure vase has. But when he sees someone point at a chamber pot or a bedpan and say, “This thing is made of gold,” he at once mistakes it for a true-gold pure vase, mistakes the excrement and urine within for pure water, and does not know that the place where a chamber pot or bedpan is set differs from the place where the Buddha is offered to. Meeting anyone, he says, “I have already seen a true-gold pure vase!” [Here name and reality are contrary, signifying that people today who use the two phrases mind-only Pure Land and self-nature Amitabha to demolish others’ recitation of the Buddha and seeking birth in the West are no different from this man.] For such people know only the name mind-only and self-nature, and do not know that mind-only and the self-nature have a vast and boundless real meaning. You should know that what is called mind-only Pure Land and self-nature Amitabha requires that one truly apply the work of Buddha-recitation, reciting until outside the mind there is no Buddha and outside the Buddha no mind, outside the mind no land and outside the land no mind, mind and Buddha non-dual, mind and land one suchness — only then is it named mind-only Pure Land and self-nature Amitabha. Such a realm — how could one who will not apply himself to Buddha-recitation even dream of it?

Now I shall briefly set my own mind-state alongside the mind-state of one who does not know fragrance from stench, purity from filth, and mistakes a chamber pot for a pure vase. Because my karmic hindrances are heavy and I have neither merit nor wisdom, though I have borne the name of a Buddha-reciter for twenty or thirty years, I have drifted and been careless, never truly applying myself single-mindedly. To have Amitabha always in mind and the Pure Land ever present is very hard to attain. Every movement of mind and thought finds it hard to escape greed, hatred, and delusion. These three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion are in truth the root of the animal, hungry ghost, and hell realms. Therefore I have often confessed: judging by our present mind-state, there is only a mind-only impure land [what appears in the mind is entirely the turbid, evil appearances of persons and self, right and wrong, and the like], and no mind-only Pure Land at all [the splendid realm of the West is rarely experienced]. There is only self-nature animal, self-nature hungry ghost, self-nature hell [because one constantly takes greed, hatred, and delusion as conditions], and truly no self-nature Amitabha [in reciting the Buddha it is not easy to attain the whole mind as the Buddha, the whole Buddha as the mind, no Buddha outside the mind, no mind outside the Buddha, mind and Buddha perfectly fused, without admixture or interval]. So it is precisely for this that I now urgently seek retirement, hoping to hide my clumsiness and await death. Though I am afflicted beyond measure, as for the ancients’ intent in using the two phrases mind-only Pure Land and self-nature Amitabha to make people recite the Buddha and surely reach thorough realization and perfect manifestation, I am confident that I can grasp it somewhat. May I ask: those today who know only the name and not the meaning, and who misapply a crucial teaching meant to urge on Buddha-recitation, using it to demolish others’ recitation — what after all is their mind-state? Is it purer than mine? If it were a little purer, I think they would not fall into such misunderstanding. My own affliction I at least know. But these parrot-people who mimic others’ words, knowing nothing of human affairs, utterly and grossly mistaken, and still pleased with themselves — the harm they do themselves and others, where can it end? Fortunately, my own teacher, the Venerable Liaogong, is deep in past roots and pure in present practice. In former years he practiced Chan and deeply accorded with the Buddha’s intent and the patriarchs’ meaning. Then he turned to Buddha-recitation and thoroughly comprehended the self-nature and mind-only. His early works, the Annotated Lamp of the Mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the Mutual Encouragement of Chan and Pure Land [the title Mutual Encouragement of Chan and Pure Land was given by the elder Yinguang], were read by the two elders Dixian and Yinguang, who praised them without stint. In recent years he has expounded the Introduction to Pure Practice, also long since published and circulated for the universal benefit of his fellows. Now, moreover, the layman Xu Huijue has compiled and edited into a volume Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light, expounding the essential meaning of the Pure Land, setting it out wholly on the tray and overturning it utterly. The whole book’s main purport takes the Buddha-fruit as its school, universally urging practitioners to enter the Buddha-fruit awakening thought after thought and to dwell in the Buddha’s right samadhi mind after mind. Such advocacy, compared with the ancients’ earnest hope that practitioners hold fast to the one phrase, the great name of Amitabha Buddha’s ten thousand virtues, and surely reach thorough realization of the mind-only Pure Land and perfect manifestation of the self-nature Amitabha — the words differ, but how does the purport differ? It may be called: ancients and moderns of one measure, the later and the earlier reflecting each other. My teacher’s exposition of the Pure Land: not a word but deeply accords with mind-only; his teaching to recite Amitabha: not a sentence but perfectly manifests the self-nature. I respectfully urge those who wish to speak of mind-only Pure Land and self-nature Amitabha to read thoroughly my teacher’s three books, written in succession. If they will not read but prattle, they cannot escape being people who do not know fragrance from stench and mistake a chamber pot for a pure vase; the discerning, hearing them, will sputter with laughter. That my teacher has expounded the wonder of the Way is shown by the three books, plain for all to see; it is not that I favor him out of partiality and can mislead people with biased praise. There is more that no one could force: I must, reluctantly, pick it out for the assembly so as to arouse right faith. My teacher of late is humble as a valley; whenever he expounds something, he asks the Buddha to attest it, and each has been answered with an auspicious response — relics obtained accordingly. Over the past year or two, those obtained one after another have been collected from time to time, twenty in all [the circumstances of their obtaining my teacher has recorded himself; I need not repeat them]. Round, moist, and radiant, they appear differently to each beholder [all who climb the mountain mostly ask to venerate them, and none fails to marvel. Moreover, a disciple most earnest and single-minded in Buddha-recitation told me that at his veneration there were fourteen. One, the largest, was like a mung bean, and on careful looking a picture of the Land of Ultimate Bliss appeared within it. This fully proves that my teacher’s pure karma is deep in merit, and that what he expounds obtains this auspicious response. Yet it still requires one whose pure karma is earnest and single-minded to be able to see such a special auspicious mark of deep merit and perfect insight. I am ashamed that my karma is heavy and I bear only the empty name of a Pure Land cultivator, while truly I am still far from pure practice. Compared with this disciple I am ashamed of myself, and compared with my teacher I truly cannot hope to reach his shoulder or back. Hence I now seek retirement, to return to the mountain and draw near him, hoping to learn a ten-thousandth part]. Were his pure karma not deep in merit and his insight not perfect and penetrating, how could this be attained? That I am now so garrulous, as if forcing people to revere and believe, is wholly because I pity myself and others who do not know the essential path out of suffering. Now, happily, my teacher’s exposition is truly a great ship of compassion in the sea of suffering of birth and death. If only everyone can read, believe, and practice, and catch up to the ship of compassion, they may sit at ease and go straight to the lotus land. “With forty-eight vows he saves sentient beings; in nine grades he brings all to the other shore” — my teacher truly acts as an envoy of the Tathagata. The layman Xu Huijue generously gave pure funds, compiled, edited and published it, asked me for a preface, and also assisted in the collation. I could not but rejoice and help it forward, and so make this rambling report, hoping that everyone will believe, accept, and practice it, and so in some ten-thousandth part repay the grace of the Dharma-milk.

Respectfully prefaced by the afflicted bhikshu Desen, at a temporary lodging in Shanghai on the eve of departure, on the Tiantian Festival [the Dragon Boat Festival] of the old calendar in the thirty-fifth year of the Republic of China.
Preface to the Circulation of Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light

I have reverently heard that the fragrance of the Tathagata’s merit and virtue and the light of his wisdom are inherent in everyone’s self-nature, and that no one lacks the slightest bit of them. It is only that we, from beginningless time, have each taken ignorance as root, karmic consciousness as trunk, false thinking as branches, afflictions as leaves, the three poisons as flowers, and all suffering as fruit. Thought after thought they sprout thickly, layer upon layer covering us over. Because of that covering, though these are inherent in the self-nature, through kalpas we have had no way to realize them. Even if one has a little good root, again, because one is born in an age of decline, with heavy karmic hindrances and shallow wisdom, one cannot by one’s own power know the mind and reach the origin, cut off delusion and verify the truth. One still drifts through the three realms, circles in the six paths, and undergoes all kinds of suffering without rest. Therefore our Shakyamuni, the World-Honored One, wishing to fulfill his own heart of pity for the age of decline, specially opened the Dharma-gate of Pure Land Buddha-recitation, borrowing Amitabha’s perfect fruit-awakening to be the causal mind of bodhi for us sentient beings. He taught us sentient beings to give rise to faith, make vows, and seek return to Ultimate Bliss. One need only, thought after thought, harbor utmost sincerity in the mind and hold fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha; when this is long and thoroughly familiar, one penetrates into the single mind. Having entered the Tathagata’s one-mind fruit-awakening, one enters the Tathagata’s pure chamber of fragrance and light, and constantly receives the Tathagata’s fragrant light of merit and wisdom, which adorns, perfumes, and illumines one. When the perfuming and illumining reach their utmost, they can cause our afflictions and karmic consciousness to melt away thought after thought, and our merit and wisdom to grow mind after mind. Even if in this life one cannot cut off all delusion and karma and personally verify the Tathagata’s real-mark fruit-awakening, if with this merit one dedicates it to the West, then at death, relying on the Buddha’s welcome, one will certainly be reborn in the Land of Bliss. In that land the realm is surpassing and the conditions strong; the power of patience is easily attained, and straight on to bodhi one swiftly perfects the Buddha-fruit. Hence the Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: hearing its sound with the ear, seeing its color with the eye, knowing its fragrance with the nose, tasting its flavor with the tongue, touching its light with the body, and taking the Dharma as the object with the mind — all attain the profoundly deep patient acceptance of the Dharma, dwell in non-retrogression, and reach the Buddha Way. Because the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation has such inconceivable, surpassing benefits, from ancient times to the present all have called it the Buddha-recitation samadhi, king among samadhis, directly receiving those of keen capacity and drawing along the middling and dull. Tathagatas of the ten directions praise it with wondrous voices; patriarchs through the ages composed treatises to proclaim it. Master Feixi of the Tang and Chan Master Miaoshen of the Ming each wrote a Treatise on the Precious King of Buddha-Recitation Samadhi. And such patriarchs as Chuandeng and Daopei wrote and continued the Treatise on Birth and No-Birth and other works, expounding the profound meaning of the samadhi — all of them perfectly beautiful and perfectly good, long transmitted and widely practiced, still extant today. Alas, we are far from the sages’ time, and people’s faculties are crude and inferior. Because the words are profound and broad and the principles subtle, many practitioners who read them in the end find it hard to grasp them on the spot; they cherish admiration in vain and have no way to enter the gate. Now there is the great Master Liaoran, who left home to cultivate and passed from Chan into Pure Land. In earlier years he wrote the Annotated Lamp of the Mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and the Mutual Encouragement of Chan and Pure Land, published together in one volume. In recent years he has resolved to seal himself in retreat and devote himself to the Buddha-recitation samadhi. Often, in the intervals of Buddha-recitation, from his own personal knowledge and personal vision he wields his brush to write, universally guiding his fellows to enter the samadhi together and all partake of its benefit and bliss. In the past several years I have gone once each year to pay respects at Lingyan and draw near to the Venerable Miao. Because the Venerable Miao is busy with temple affairs and has no leisure for much talk, I repeatedly went to the retreat gate to ask the Master for instruction. Through the Master’s compassion and earnest guidance I drank sweet dew and gained much. Last year I joined the intensive seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat and was graciously admitted into the retreat chamber, where I bowed and read his Treatise on the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi, the Jewel King That Emerges from the World, and the records of his talks and instructions in the Buddha-recitation hall. The words are clear, the principles thorough. Cause and fruit interpenetrate; provisional and real are one. It is at once sudden and perfect, at once perfect and sudden. Those of keen capacity awaken on the spot and enter the Buddha-fruit real-mark middle way; the middling and dull likewise, through utmost sincerity, enter gradually and deeply. Every sentence flows naturally from the mind of Buddha-recitation; with provisional skill and expedient means, with similes and indications, it makes things easy to grasp and draws one in unawares, leading later students on and bringing them boundless benefit. Even should a follower of Chan or of the teachings not believe in reciting the Buddha and seeking birth in the West, if he happens to leaf through this book, it is sure to make him deeply believe and long for it. Why? Because the Master takes Amitabha’s fruit-awakening as his school. The Tathagata’s real-mark fruit-awakening excludes no dharma and fuses with no dharma; though it does not take in Chan and the teachings as such, there is nothing in it that does not accord with Chan and the teachings. It is originally principle just as it is fact, fact just as it is principle; fact and principle perfectly fused, the very body is the Buddha-fruit. Even one who neither believes nor practices can hardly escape beyond the Buddha-fruit, for the Buddha-fruit is perfect and encompasses all without remainder. After the Master entered the perfect principle of the Buddha-fruit, looking back on his former dual practice of Chan and Pure Land, he felt it to be like two things joined together; better to put down the whole body, be utterly sincere thought after thought, and dwell at ease in the Buddha-fruit, holding the Buddha’s name, relying on the Buddha’s nurture — whole and perfectly fused, ready-made and effortless. What need for dual practice? How lofty this wondrous thesis, how perfect and thorough! Truly it may be said: the three capacities are universally gathered, the keen and the dull wholly received; in the sea of suffering of the Saha world another ship of compassion is added, carrying all who recite the Buddha together to the other shore of the Land of Bliss. Reverently reading the treatise and seeing his vow to save beings, one sees enough to show my teacher’s earnest compassion and profound vow-power. Whenever the Master wields his brush to write in the still of the night, he constantly receives the Buddha’s blessing, and repeatedly relics have descended from the lamp, a dozen or so in all, each like a pearl, differing in color and light, differing in size. I personally was able to venerate them, and my joy was boundless; I could not but join my palms and exclaim: How wonderful, how rare! This is exactly as the Master says: the jewel king of samadhi surpasses all worldly treasures; its light penetrates everywhere, standing alone and perfectly manifest. Now with this proof my faith is deeper still. Then I reflected: since first we had birth and death, we have long dwelt in the Saha world through kalpas as many as dust motes, deluded and unknowing. Today, instructed by the Master, I first know that we turbid, inferior ordinary beings are originally within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening real mind, neither going out nor coming in. Is this not to obtain what was never obtained, to hear what was never heard — rarely met in a thousand lives, hard to encounter in ten thousand kalpas? From then on, reciting the Buddha, I gradually find a savor in it. And looking at my afflictions and karmic consciousness, I find them gradually lightening, no longer like the raging waves of before; I begin to see a little calm. Reflecting on this benefit: had I not wholly relied on Amitabha’s perfect fruit-awakening to nurture and sustain me, and on the power of the Tathagata’s fragrant light to perfume and illumine me, how could I have had such capacity? Since the jewel king of samadhi brings immeasurable benefit, and to obtain this perfuming cultivation is no shallow causal connection, how dare I, having been perfumed and illumined, keep the benefit to myself alone? Therefore, respectfully following the profound and wondrous purport the Master has shown, and the causal connection of my drawing near him, and even my reverent viewing of the relics, which deeply increased my faith, I have gathered these several threads into a humble essay, and with difficulty collected pure funds to publish and circulate it. I universally vow that Pure Land friends of the ten directions may together cultivate the Buddha-recitation samadhi, hoping that in this life each may be steeped in the fragrance of the Tathagata’s merit and virtue and warmed by the light of his wisdom, and at the end of life return together to Ultimate Bliss, each seated high on a jeweled lotus. I too, by this slight cause, make vows and dedicate them to the West, praying now that my pure karma be soon accomplished, that at death I depart in peace, personally welcomed by Amitabha, in a snap of the fingers entering the lotus land, ever near Amitabha to learn, swiftly realizing the real mark of bodhi. Then, following the Master, I will return to the Saha world, always attend him, and help spread the teaching. Thus the Buddha’s grace and the teacher’s grace are both repaid, and self and others are saved together. Should a reader doubt, saying, “The pure chamber of fragrance and light has no door — from where, after all, does one enter?”, I have constantly heard the Master say: The nature of awakening is all-pervading and complete; beings and Buddhas are one body; the ten realms dwell together — who is outside the chamber? It is only because of long delusion and non-awakening that one falsely sees a going out and coming in. It is like a drunkard who, because his mind is clouded, falsely sees mountain forests though he is inside the house. If one can accept it with a single thought right now, one is at peace wherever one is; originally one neither goes out nor comes in, dwelling in the Buddha’s right samadhi. The Master has also said: with one thought of utmost sincerity, one enters in one thought; with every thought of utmost sincerity, one enters in every thought. And: with one thought unmoving, one dwells for one thought; with every thought unmoving, one dwells for every thought. This is what is meant by entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light. To understand it otherwise is not only to fail the Buddha’s grace but also to mistake the Master’s profound intent. May all my fellows calm their spirits and read it, consider it with right mindfulness, and not be careless. So may we together enter the assembly of the Buddha-fruit right samadhi and together receive the benefit of the perfuming light of fragrance. I write these reasons here as a preface.

Respectfully prefaced, with palms joined, by the white-robed attendant Xu Huijue, in the Chamber of Fragrance and Light of the Bodhi Garden at Yinxi Town, Taicang County, on the birthday of Maitreya Bodhisattva in the first month of the thirty-fifth year of the Republic of China.
Author’s Preface to Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light

I have often reflected that Shakyamuni, the World-Honored One, out of a thorough compassion pitied the beings of the age of decline — shallow in faculties, darkened in knowledge, unable by their own power to know the mind and reach the origin, cut off delusion and verify the truth, and pass beyond the three realms; ever in the Saha world, circling in the six paths, undergoing all suffering with no way out. Therefore he specially opened the one gate of the Pure Land: of borrowing the fruit to cultivate the cause, of relying on the Buddha for rebirth. First he spoke of the splendor of the dependent and proper retribution of Ultimate Bliss; next he taught the arising of faith and the making of vows, and the holding fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha for one day up to seven days, in the hope of attaining single-mindedness. Looking at these causes and conditions, there is within them a profoundly wondrous purport, inconceivable. Yet practitioners read without noticing, and few grasp it. What is this profoundly wondrous purport? The single-mindedness the Buddha speaks of is the original awakening that is the common source of sages and ordinary beings, the true mind that is one substance with beings and Buddhas. If we are willing, thought after thought, to harbor utmost sincerity in the mind and hold fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha, it can cause us, thought after thought, to turn from dust and accord with awakening, to turn the false back to the true — like rivers entering the sea, entering gradually and deeply, until our own mind melts into the Buddha’s mind and the Buddha’s mind merges with our own. Moreover, this single-mindedness is the perfect fruit-awakening that Amitabha has verified. And this single-mindedness is the Buddha-recitation samadhi that we sentient beings have lost. If we are willing, thought after thought, to harbor utmost sincerity in the mind and hold fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha, it can cause us, thought after thought, to penetrate the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening and dwell at ease in the Tathagata’s real-mark right samadhi. It is like broken gold cast into a furnace, which can gradually melt and merge into one body. We who recite the Buddha are likewise. Entering the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening, not only are we not turned about by all the dust-toil and karmic consciousness, but we can cause all dust-toil and karmic consciousness gradually to melt away. When the melting reaches its utmost, it at last becomes one piece. When a single thought becomes one piece, scatteredness of itself is gone. Scatteredness gone, right samadhi appears [in Sanskrit, samadhi; here it means right samadhi]. If we can, thought after thought, enter the Buddha’s perfect fruit-awakening and, mind after mind, dwell in the Buddha’s real-mark right samadhi, and not retreat to the end of life, then the work of pure karma will certainly be accomplished. With pure karma accomplished, the golden platform may be awaited seated, the jeweled pool may be entrusted with our birth. And when death approaches, naturally the turbid evil of the Saha world does not appear, and the splendid realm of the Pure Land shines clear. The Buddha is moved to welcome us in person, and in a moment we arrive. Is this not called attaining birth at death as one wishes — effortless and easy? Looking through the great sages and worthies of old, whose auspicious signs at death were brilliant, who died sitting or standing at their own will, going when they wished to go and needing no one’s help to go — none of them failed to obtain this from the Buddha-recitation samadhi. But of practitioners today, though they arouse the mind to recite the Buddha, many do not understand the Buddha’s intent. They take this single-mindedness to belong wholly to their own arising-and-ceasing false mind, having nothing to do with the Buddha. Therefore those who recite the Buddha, wishing to accomplish the single mind, in the end never attain it. It is what is called: the more you knead it, the more it scatters; the more you grasp it, the more it tangles. Examining the cause of this, it mostly comes from over-clinging to Yongming’s Four Brief Analyses, doubting that this Amitabha one-mind perfect fruit-awakening can be deeply entered and dwelt in, fearing that one will fall into Chan concentration and turn it into self-power, and so fail of rebirth. For this reason many cast it aside. Having abandoned Amitabha’s one-mind perfect fruit-awakening, when such a practitioner recites the Buddha he can never settle his mind and take his stand, like a fish in shallow water lacking nurture. It is precisely that he lacks other-power; and one who wishes to settle body and life and be free to go or stay — is he not straining to the utmost? Hence it is said: the true and the false are each distinct, the provisional and the real separated. One abandons the real and follows the provisional, and clings to the provisional as the real. Though he arouses the mind to hold the name, from first to last he never accords with the Buddha’s intent, and all his life sits guarding the gate of the first step, unwilling to advance and enter deeply into the Tathagata’s adorned jewel-realm. Those whom the Tathagata constantly calls pitiable are precisely this kind. If one wished to urge them to advance deeper, they would surely be like the poor son at the Lotus assembly, unable to avoid crying out in complaint: “I have committed no crime; why do you seize me?” They do not realize that the provisional aspect of Amitabha’s name and the real aspect of the one-mind fruit-awakening are from the first perfectly fused without obstruction, real and one suchness, neither identical nor apart, neither within nor without. Vast and boundless, their measure the same as the Dharma-realm. The empty space of the ten directions they wholly contain. They gather in all beings of the nine realms, not one of whom is outside them. Having abandoned the real of the one-mind fruit-awakening and clung one-sidedly to the provisional of Amitabha’s name, even if one gains benefit, in the end it is shallow and small, and so the enjoyment at death is also small. One who wishes to dissolve the heavy karmic hindrances accumulated through kalpas, and at death rely on the Buddha’s welcome to be reborn in the Land of Bliss — is he not straining with all his might and still finding it hard? It is like bathing: with little water and heavy grime, it is hard to be clean. To be clean all over, one must sit with the whole body in the bath, gradually perfumed and steeped, washed for a long time, and only then can it all be removed without remainder. We who recite the Buddha are likewise. If only we can enter the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening, then from then on we constantly receive the Buddha’s power added to us and the Dharma’s power fusing with us. When the fusion reaches its utmost, the whole body is complete, naturally unscattered and unconfused, dwelling at ease in right samadhi. It is like an unborn child still in the mother’s womb, the whole body seated within the mother’s belly, relying on the mother’s nurture, gradually growing to full term. We who recite the Buddha are likewise. Entering the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening and dwelling at ease in the Tathagata’s real-mark right samadhi, one may say that the whole body is seated within the Tathagata’s Dharmakaya, relying on the Buddha’s nurture, so that the practitioner’s boundless karmic hindrances gradually dissolve and his immeasurable merit and wisdom secretly grow. This is what is called borrowing the fruit to accomplish the cause, and, as cause, dwelling in the fruit; adorning oneself with the Buddha’s adornment and sustaining oneself with the Buddha’s sustaining. Attaining this perfuming cultivation, the benefit is immeasurable; even if in this life one cannot cut off delusion and personally realize it, on arriving in the West the causal ground is also strong, and advancing gradually from there one may swiftly realize the Buddha-fruit. What was said above — that the World-Honored One taught people to arouse faith, make vows, and hold fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha from one day up to seven days in the hope of attaining single-mindedness, and that within this there lies a profoundly wondrous purport, inconceivable — this is that inconceivable, profoundly wondrous benefit. Apart from those practitioners who are full of doubt and discrimination, the rest — simple men and women — need no further guidance, for they grasp it at a touch. It is like farmers in the mountains and wilds who have never once gone out of doors and know nothing at all of the world’s affairs: they only understand eating at home each day and working in the fields, and naturally great matters are accomplished and the five grains ripen in abundance. The foolish who recite the Buddha are likewise. Of all the scriptures and teachings they know nothing, yet the one gate of Buddha-recitation alone they can take up directly, with no doubt or discrimination. Thought after thought harboring utmost sincerity and holding fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha, they naturally accord with the Buddha’s perfect fruit-awakening, secretly and invisibly. Why? Because the causal mind of beings and the fruit-awakening of the Buddha are from the first not separated by a hair’s breadth. It is like a bubble merging into water, naturally in accord. Where there is no accord, it is all because the practitioner falsely arouses doubt and falsely gives rise to discrimination, unwilling to put down the whole body and, dying to the mind, to enter. Thus the causal mind of beings and the fruit-awakening of the Buddha, the true and the false, are each distinct, self and other separated. Though he is within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening real mind, he dares not accept it thought after thought, and is as far off as a thousand or ten thousand li. This is exactly the saying: the Buddha does not distance himself from people; people distance themselves from the Buddha. Does the Buddha’s eye, seeing all around, not pity them? Perhaps someone asks: By what the Master has said, is this not the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land? The answer is: No. Why? Amitabha’s bodhi fruit-awakening is from the first perfect in merit and wisdom, provisional and real one suchness. One who understands the provisional knows the provisional and returns from the provisional to the real. One who sees the real sees the real, and the provisional itself is the real. Only do not doubt and discriminate; one need only, thought after thought, keep sincerity and hold fast to the Buddha’s name, and even simple men and women can be made, in the present moment, to enter thought after thought, entering gradually and deeply. What need is there of dual practice? If without the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land your awakening is incomplete, as if missing half, then you wrongly blame Amitabha Buddha for having in former times, on his causal ground, cultivated only merit and not wisdom. Examine this carefully: is there any such principle? It is said: all Buddhas share the same Way, originally without a second difference. Because merit and wisdom are already perfect, one is named a Buddha. All the Buddhas of the ten directions are without exception thus. How could Amitabha Buddha alone be otherwise? I only wish that the benevolent one would consider this well, and not misunderstand, deluding himself and deluding others. Since I entered the retreat, more than three years have passed without my noticing, urging people to enter the Buddha-fruit together and cultivate the Buddha-recitation samadhi together. Over the years all my discourses have been recorded in full. Each time a piece was finished, I offered it before the Buddha and asked the Buddha’s blessing and gracious attestation, and by the Buddha’s compassion each was granted an auspicious response. Of all these discourses, apart from the Treatise on the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi, the Jewel King That Emerges from the World, the rest were all spoken in this temple’s Buddha-recitation hall during a session of intensive practice, recorded one after another, and gradually accumulated into a volume. Last spring, when the layman Xu Huijue of Taicang came to the mountain to collect and print my Introduction to Pure Practice, I had already given this treatise to him to read. Having read it, he joyfully said: the Buddha-recitation samadhi is the portion of everyone; each and all may enter it. From this it is clear that the layman’s past roots are deep, for he grasped the treatise well and had few doubts. So last winter he again raised funds separately, intending to print this book. Now, seeing that the pieces after the treatise are gathered in as well, he is all the more delighted and satisfied, and reads them over and over. Having read them, he bowed reverently and exclaimed: Excellent! The Buddha-recitation samadhi is, it turns out, the Pure Land school’s own important family inheritance, its value surpassing the mani jewel, rarely met in a thousand lives, hard to encounter in ten thousand kalpas. Now that we have met it, how dare we let it pass? The disciple is resolved to print and circulate it next year, universally forming pure connections, vowing that all lotus friends may together win its surpassing benefit. The disciple too, by this slight good root, may dedicate it to the Ultimate Bliss Pure Land, hoping that after birth in the West he may always follow the Master in attending the Compassionate Honored One, drawing near and learning, and swiftly realize bodhi. Then, following the Master and riding again the wheel of vows, he may return to the Saha world and help transform all sentient beings. Because he saw the layman’s vast resolve and true, earnest faith and vows, he has already, in advance of next year, made paper plates himself and printed a thousand copies, after which more copies may be printed as people are moved to contribute, for wide circulation. He further asked me for a preface and requested me to name the book, so I could not but rejoice and consent, to fulfill his wish. Therefore I briefly set out the outline here to inform my fellows universally. Though the writing is plain and homely, the meaning has something worth taking. Further, considering the meaning of the whole book, it takes the Buddha-fruit as its special school, universally urging those who recite the Buddha to enter the Buddha-fruit awakening thought after thought, to dwell in the Buddha’s right samadhi mind after mind, to hold fast to the sacred name of Amitabha, and at death to be welcomed by the Buddha. Seeing this profound and wondrous purport, the whole should be titled Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light. Why? The Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening is wholly formed by the adornment of merit and wisdom, possessing the fragrance of immeasurable merit and virtue and the light of immeasurable wisdom, filling the fruit-awakening, real and one suchness. If we are willing, thought after thought, to hold fast to the name of Amitabha Buddha, we shall naturally, thought after thought, penetrate the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening and dwell at ease in the Tathagata’s real-mark right samadhi. Constantly receiving the Tathagata’s fragrant light of merit and wisdom to nurture, sustain, perfume, and illumine us throughout the body, it can cause all dust-toil and karmic consciousness gradually to melt away. When the melting reaches its utmost, all is transformed into the great treasury of light of the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awakening. Wholly penetrating, all becomes one color. This is what is called borrowing the fruit to penetrate the cause, and by the cause revealing the fruit. It exactly matches the sutra’s words: without recourse to expedient means, one of oneself opens the mind; like a person steeped in incense whose body bears its fragrance, this is called adorned with Fragrance and Light. Therefore it is named Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light. May those who read this book, seeing this title, reflect on its meaning, arouse the mind to read it, fix their attention and ponder it, and cultivate by perfume-drenching in accord with the Dharma: deeply entering the Buddha-fruit, dwelling in the Buddha’s right samadhi, and being welcomed by the Buddha. Reborn thus, a thousand out of a thousand are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred. Not only is the layman’s merit inconceivable, but by this propagation the Buddha’s own heart is also gladdened, the Dharma-gate gains luster, and practitioners are greatly fortunate. I humbly pray that by the blessing of the Three Jewels’ majestic spiritual power, and by the strength of their nurturing and sustaining, the nation’s foundation be forever firm, the world at peace, the wind and rain timely, and the people happy. And this small heart of dedication and vow I have recorded in this rough essay and named a preface.

the twelfth month of the thirty-fourth year of the Republic of China, on the day of Shakyamuni’s enlightenment — prefaced by Liaoran, the monk fed on gruel and rice at Lingyan, in the Non-retreat Chamber of the Zhen Peach Garden of the Sea of the Buddha’s Spring.

What are the three? The first is the mind of utmost sincerity; the second is the deep mind; the third is the mind of dedication and vows. With this merit one dedicates and vows, seeking birth in Ultimate Bliss, and one’s grade will certainly be high. Why?
