Again, for one who recites the Buddha, the mind that can recite is self-power, and the Buddha recited is other-power. Thus, when self-power and other-power are attended to together, it is the easier to have response and spiritual communion, to receive the Buddha’s guidance, to transcend the three realms horizontally, and to be reborn in the Land of Bliss. This is not like practicing Chan, which relies on self-power alone to know the mind and reach the source, cut off delusion and realize the truth, and transcend the three realms vertically. What is meant by attending to self-power and other-power together is this: the practitioner must himself have a portion of true, earnest cultivation before he can obtain a portion of the other-power’s true benefit. If in his own cultivation he makes no true effort at all, then the other-power also has no place to be applied. It is like a poor child wandering and begging with no fixed dwelling: though the elder has the mind to give, he cannot make him receive it. Pure practitioners are likewise. With a drifting, aimless practice, it is hard to move the Buddha’s power to add to one, the Dharma-power to fuse with one, to eliminate karmic hindrances now, and to rely on the Buddha for rebirth at the end.

As for the subtle, wondrous benefit within Amitabha Buddha’s bodhi sea: it is originally adorned with ten thousand virtues, and its benefit is inexhaustible. Beings seek it through kalpas without end. But because our faculties are great or small, our practice diligent or lazy, our effort concentrated or scattered, the benefit each obtains differs in depth, in quantity, and in speed. It is like the waters of the four great oceans: let all the beings of the great earth drink of them, and in the end they cannot be exhausted. From the asura kings above to the tiniest insects below, each can only be filled according to its belly, and in the end none can reach the bottom. Amitabha Buddha’s bodhi fruit-sea is likewise: all beings of the nine realms may drink of it, and in the end it cannot be exhausted. Only a Buddha with a Buddha can drain it in a single draught, with nothing left over. Why? Because all Buddhas and Tathagatas have already perfectly broken ignorance and perfectly verified the real-mark fruit-sea. Bodhisattvas, though they verify it, have not perfected it; the Two Vehicles, though they verify it, verify it partially; ordinary beings, though they possess it, are deluded and have never been aware of it. Even if they can understand and become aware, what can they do when delusion and karma are not yet removed? Inwardly their illumination seems to be freed, yet when facing objects they are still deluded — like a cracked vessel that scatters when it meets water. If one day they lose their footing, they still have a share in falling. If they fall into the three evil paths, for a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives they will not hear the Buddha’s name. Therefore, whether wise or foolish, all should have faith and vows and recite the Buddha. The keen-rooted awaken in this present life and enter deep into Amitabha’s bodhi fruit-sea. Those of middling and lesser faculties, though not yet awakened, need only possess true faith and earnest vows, keep sincerity in the mind thought after thought, and hold Amitabha Buddha’s name; this can bring them gradually to accord with the Tathagata’s bodhi fruit-sea, and they too will be received by the Tathagata’s bodhi fruit-sea and all his vow-powers, all gathered home to the Land of Lotuses.

Indeed, we beings, through countless kalpas, have always been within Amitabha Buddha’s bodhi mind, right up to this day, and have never departed from it. But because we have always been deluded, unaware and unknowing, and do not understand how to recite the Buddha and seek birth in the Land of Bliss, therefore, though we are within the Tathagata’s bodhi mind, we pass a thousand myriads of kalpas and in the end gain no benefit. If we now can truly believe deeply that we are beings within Amitabha’s bodhi mind, then from this cultivation we shall gradually feel that we have something to rely upon, and it will be easier than before. Like a dragon dwelling in the sea, contained within the water of its own nature: thought after thought we have support, step by step we tread solid ground. When we wish to walk, we walk; when we wish to stop, we stop. Self-power and other-power suddenly feel intimate — like water meeting water, an accord by nature, the whole body one suchness, not the slightest separation. Whatever we cultivate never goes outside Amitabha Buddha’s bodhi mind. When reciting the Buddha, we feel of ourselves that every phrase of the Buddha-name flows out from the Tathagata’s bodhi mind, and again we feel that every phrase of the Buddha-name returns into the Tathagata’s bodhi mind, fused and perfect, pervading the Dharma-realm. Obtaining this nurture, we constantly receive the Buddha’s power added to us and the Dharma-power fusing with us, like hot water melting snow, like a furnace melting gold. It can cause our boundless karmic hindrances to be gradually dissolved and our immeasurable merit and wisdom to grow unseen. This is precisely what is meant by adorning oneself with the Buddha’s adornment and upholding oneself with the Buddha’s upholding. We wait only until the Saha reward is finished and the Western conditions are ripe: then suddenly, within the Tathagata’s bodhi mind, excellent scenes shine forth and appear before our eyes. Even though there be mountains, forests, and houses, at that time there is no hindrance at all. With open eyes we see it, with closed eyes we see it. By the Buddha’s spiritual power, in the snap of a finger we arrive. Is not this inconceivable, supremely excellent benefit the very accord of faculty and teaching, the union of mind and nature, like space according with space, like water joining water — when the accord reaches its utmost, at last becoming a piece; one thought a piece, self and other one suchness — obtained through the three inconceivable powers completing one another? This is the meaning of attending to self-power and other-power together.

What is it not to neglect either? It means that when self-power and other-power are joined, results come easily, but when one is favored, pure karma is hard to accomplish. Even if it can be accomplished, the benefit is very small. Someone may say he does not believe that favoring one makes pure karma hard to accomplish — what proof is there? I shall set it out below. For several decades, in every situation and circumstance I have met, whenever I recall them now they are perfectly clear, as if before my eyes. I have often seen certain practitioners who, hearing that in Shakyamuni Tathagata’s teaching for one age all Dharma-gates rely wholly on self-power, and only the Pure Land Dharma-gate relies wholly on the Buddha’s power, therefore pay no attention at all to self-power. If one occasionally mentions it to them, see how they misunderstand, fearing to fall into Chan practice and become self-power, betray the Buddha’s grace, and fail of rebirth. So one must explain to them one by one: know that the self-power of Buddha-recitation is quite different from the self-power of Chan practice. Why? Chan practice takes one’s own mind as its sole doctrine — all is mind only. Buddha-recitation takes the Buddha’s mind as its sole doctrine — all is Buddha only. Since it takes the Buddha’s mind as its doctrine and all is Buddha only, the practitioner of Buddha-recitation always takes the Buddha’s mind as his home, and whenever he recites the Buddha he feels that he is originally a being within Amitabha’s mind. Since he is a being within Amitabha’s mind, he should, thought after thought, dwell at ease in the Buddha’s mind, recite the Buddha with a settled mind, and not drift. If he feels himself drifting, he should gather it and make it return. This is what is meant by attending to self-power and other-power together.

Moreover, Chan practice must attain concentration and then open wisdom; Buddha-recitation need only seek concentration, and that is enough. What is meant by seeking only concentration? It is to attain single-mindedness, undisturbed. For this single mind is the Tathagata’s true bodhi mind. Only on entering the Tathagata’s true bodhi mind can one, thought after thought, dwell in the Buddha’s right samadhi and, compared with ordinary recitation, have something to rely on, so that every phrase of the Buddha-name feels powerful. Not only is one no longer turned about by all the dusts of affliction and karmic consciousness — one can instead cause all the dusts of affliction and karmic consciousness gradually to dissolve. When the dissolution reaches its utmost, at last it becomes a piece. When one thought becomes a piece, scattering vanishes of itself, and with scattering gone, right samadhi appears. Moreover, Chan practice requires investigating Chan; Buddha-recitation requires only simple recitation. Moreover, Chan practice looks only to self-power; Buddha-recitation attends to self-power and Buddha-power together. If they are not attended to together, then though the mouth recites the Buddha, the mind drifts, and because it cannot unite with the Buddha’s power, the benefit obtained also lacks strength. If the present benefit lacks strength, will the benefit at death instead have strength? It is said that the Pure Land Dharma-gate relies wholly on the Buddha’s power — that is of course so. But if you cling too far and neglect self-power, the Buddha’s power is hard to rely on. As the saying goes: a sheepskin is warm, but it does not warm a man with no breath in him. It is the same here: however efficacious the Buddha-Dharma, it is not efficacious for one who neglects self-power. Without self-power, with what shall one apply effort and cultivate? Without other-power, from what shall one settle the mind and take one’s stand? Only like a fish in water can one settle body and life and move or stay at will. Self-power and other-power are not separated by a hair; if you part them, both lose their function. Hence it is said that self-power and other-power must not be neglected either one. Explaining it thus to them one by one, they then gladly believe and accept, without giving rise to a single doubt.

Again we see certain practitioners whose misunderstanding is even greater. Because they read in the Essentials of the Amitabha Sutra: “Whether one is reborn depends entirely on whether faith and vows are present; the height of one’s grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the name,” they conclude that the Pure Land Dharma-gate is extremely easy: with faith and vows, one may recite the Buddha casually, and at death, relying on the Buddha’s guidance, one will certainly be reborn — the lower grade at least is secure. And because they read in the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations: “The ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes, with a tenfold recitation at the end of life, are received and guided by the Buddha and reborn carrying their karma,” they therefore let body, mouth, and mind run loose as conditions allow, with little restraint and little mindful awareness. They constantly create karma and feel no remorse after doing so. Or they say: “So-and-so recited the Buddha casually, not even two years, but his faith and vows were genuine and his auspicious signs at death were quite good; he was reborn.” Therefore they pay no attention at all to their own pure-karma practice. Though they recite the Buddha, it is more empty than real. They do not ask whether their effort has strength, whether their feet are planted firm. Drifting and wandering along, they do not notice that they are gradually growing old. When the great limit arrives, a foul disease comes upon the body, medicine and doctors are of no avail, no means of rescue remains; they call for father and mother, moaning on the sickbed, the illness long drawn out with no knowing when it will end. They cannot seek life, they cannot seek death. One who has a conscience, at this point, feels remorse and regret, and only then knows that in the days of health he did not himself strive in the work of Buddha-recitation. So it is that by today the benefit has no strength at all: karmic hindrances appear before him, the mind is hard to master, he is inverted and confused, utterly without support. Though the Buddha is compassionate, he cannot save me. Until he reaches the extreme of confusion, even though others recite the Buddha beside him, he is unaware and unknowing, and drifts vaguely, dimly away. What a pity that the practice that could have ended birth and death in this life becomes only a distant cause for later lives. One who has no conscience, meeting his own unbearable pain, instead gives rise to slander, saying the Buddha-Dharma deceives people and he no longer believes. If someone urges him to recite the Buddha so that at death he may move the Buddha to come and welcome him, he says: “I do not see the Buddha anywhere.” Because of this crime of slandering the Three Jewels, after death he will certainly fall into the evil paths. Alas, what a pity! All because of a single mistaken thought at the beginning, from which he never knew how to turn back, he turns the supreme good cause that could in this life end birth and death, transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, and go on to Buddhahood, forever enjoying wondrous bliss, into an evil fruit of a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives of suffering in the three evil paths. If we now trace its cause, is it not all because of that single mistaken thought at the beginning, from which he never knew how to turn back — not understanding that self and other must be attended to together and that subject and object complete each other, but holding to one and discarding the other, deficient in his own cultivation, and then blaming the Buddha-Dharma for deceiving him?

Since I left home, I have passed many years; what I have seen with my eyes and heard with my ears I shall not forget while I live. Often when I think of it, my heart trembles and my hair stands on end, tears fall and wet my collar, and my shame and dismay are beyond measure. From this I first knew that the two words faith and vows can only be a guide; they cannot be taken as the actual practice. Faith and vows are like the eyes seeing; Buddha-recitation is like the feet walking. Therefore the ancients classified faith and vows as the practice of wisdom and holding the name as the practice of action. The practice of wisdom is what one already knows and sees; the practice of action requires that the feet walk before one can arrive there. Reading this makes it clearer still, and gives one solid ground. If one does not oneself strive in cultivation and gradually plant one’s feet firm while awaiting the Buddha’s welcome, but relies merely on a little faith and vows, on the Buddha’s guidance at death, and on rebirth while carrying one’s karma, in the end it is not secure. Though such people are not altogether lacking, it is not something everyone can attain: among ten million, how few are found. Only those who in former lives planted lotus causes and have been deeply cultivated are exempt from this rule. Looking through the ancients, their auspicious signs at death were manifest, so that people could see and hear them; dying seated or standing, at their own will; wishing to go, they went, and went without needing anyone’s help — all of this came from the three inconceivable powers completing one another. Hence it is said that self-power and other-power must be attended to together and neither neglected; and this covers this profound and wondrous purport. May all companions in purity take heed, reflect, perfume and cultivate according to the Dharma, and together enter the fruit-sea. How fortunate for the Dharma-gate, how fortunate for our fellows.
Often Reading the Amitabha Sutra, One Feels It Exceedingly Wondrous

The sutra says: “If a good man or good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha and holds his name, whether for one day, for two days, or even for seven days, single-mindedly and undisturbed, then when that person is about to die, Amitabha Buddha with all the sages will appear before him.” Reading again and again to this point, I pay heed and observe, reflecting with right mindfulness, and I feel that this passage of causal connection is subtle and wondrous to the utmost, bringing a joy hard to express. What is this subtlety? I shall set it out below. This causal connection is just like digging a pond to await the moon: gradually the water fills and becomes a pond. When the fine night of the fifteenth comes, the clouds that block the sky suddenly scatter all at once, and unawares the full moon in the pond appears of itself. Digging a pond stands for our hearing of the land of Ultimate Bliss in the West, its proper and dependent adornments and its inexhaustible wondrous bliss; from this we give rise to faith and vows, and though our consciousness has not yet gone, our faith and vows have already reached the West. Awaiting the moon stands for our hope that at the end of life the Buddha will come to welcome us. The water gradually filling to become a pond stands for our now, thought after thought keeping sincerity in the mind, holding Amitabha Buddha’s name, gradually according with the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness and dwelling at ease in the Tathagata’s real-mark right samadhi — like water returning to water, gradually feeling full, one’s own mind melting into the Buddha’s mind and the Buddha’s mind merging into one’s own. The fine night of the fifteenth stands for the time of our death. The clouds blocking the sky scattering all at once stands for all the various dusts of affliction and karmic consciousness in our breast at that time suddenly opening at once, without the least attachment or hindrance. The full moon in the pond appearing of itself unawares stands for our, originally within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, seeing with our own eyes the Tathagata’s marks and excellences, his hand outstretched to receive and guide us. The text then says: “When that person’s life ends, with a mind not inverted, he at once attains rebirth in Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.” When that person’s life ends, with a mind not inverted, means that at that time our right mindfulness dwells within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, like the bright sun in the sky, shining unfailingly, perfectly clear, giving rise to not a single thought of inversion or scattered fancy. He at once attains rebirth in Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss means that the Land of Bliss, though separated from the Saha world by a hundred thousand million lands, is originally within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, not a hair’s breadth away; by the Buddha’s spiritual power, in the snap of a finger one arrives. Because I have read to this point again and again, observing and reflecting, and reflecting without cease, I suddenly felt my body within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, dwelling at ease in right samadhi, thus and unmoved, fused and perfect, pervading the Dharma-realm. And I reflected further: if practitioners of Buddha-recitation could each borrow this to perfume and cultivate, then though in the present they cannot cut off delusion and personally verify, at the end of life the cause would still be strong.

From this I first knew that the four words single-mindedness, undisturbed are the fruit-awareness right samadhi of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Buddha-recitation samadhi of the beings of the nine realms. They are thorough above and below, most sudden and most perfect. The whole great causal matter of perfecting the Buddha-fruit above and saving beings below lies entirely within them, lacking not a hair. Their bearing is immense, most weighty and most essential; through the end of the future one cannot exhaust their praise. All who cultivate should take deep note and not read them casually. Why? To read them casually is this: ordinary practitioners, reading these four words single-mindedness, undisturbed, take them wholly as their own birth-and-death false mind, and hope to make it a piece and undisturbed. They do not know that their own birth-and-death false mind is illusory and impermanent, without true nature. If one does not borrow the containing, nurturing, upholding, and fusing power of the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real wondrous mind, how can one make it a piece and undisturbed? That is why, when most people begin to recite the Buddha, it is for the most part a single false mind, like a monkey that cannot be tamed, and they do not know how to make it free and at peace. What is meant by our now wishing to make our own false monkey-mind obedient and tamed, free and at peace? We must borrow the containing, nurturing, upholding, and fusing power of the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real wondrous mind; only then can it gradually become obedient, gradually be tamed, and when long matured, naturally be unscattered and undisturbed, free and at peace. For example, in the dog days of the sixth month, when fierce heat presses on one and the mind is ill at ease: if one suddenly runs into a cool pond and bathes the whole body, at once one feels cool within and without — is not body and mind then at ease? Practitioners of Buddha-recitation are likewise. When the afflictions of the six dusts blaze and press upon one and the mind is ill at ease, if one suddenly gains entry into the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness cool ocean and is wholly nurtured, at once one feels cool within and without, and body and mind are at ease. Again, like the freezing days of the twelfth month, when bitter cold presses on one and the mind is not at peace: if one suddenly runs into the great warm sunlight and is wholly warmed and shone upon, at once one feels warm within and without — is not body and mind then at peace? Practitioners of Buddha-recitation are likewise. When the coverings of the five aggregates obstruct and press upon one and the mind is not at peace, if one suddenly gains entry into the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness great treasury of light and is wholly fused within it, at once one feels light within and without, and body and mind are at peace. Having gained ease and peace, from then on the false mind gradually becomes obedient, gradually is tamed; and when taming reaches its utmost, it is naturally controlled without control.

What is the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness? The two words single mind spoken above are precisely the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness. The two words undisturbed are precisely our beings’ birth-and-death false mind. If we can, thought after thought, keep sincerity in the mind and hold Amitabha Buddha’s name, it can cause our birth-and-death false mind, unseen and unknowing, naturally and gradually to accord with the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, dwell at ease in right samadhi, thus and unmoved, fused and perfect, pervading the Dharma-realm; hence it is called single-mindedness, undisturbed. Know that we, through countless kalpas, have always been within Amitabha Buddha’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, right up to this day, and have never departed from it — but because we have always been deluded, unaware and unknowing. Seen with the right eye, apart from the Buddha alone, who has perfectly verified the fruit-awareness, all beings of the nine realms are within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, borrowing the fruit to cultivate the cause. Why? Because this single mind has a general and a particular aspect. Generally speaking, sages and ordinary beings are originally of one source, and beings and Buddhas are one substance. Particularly speaking, the stations of beings and Buddhas differ vastly, each person distinct, each one different. Why? If we speak of the ultimate single mind, only the Buddha alone has verified it, perfectly breaking ignorance and perfectly verifying real mark. It is like a solar eclipse: because the whole is already perfectly manifest and the entire body has recovered its light, it is called the ultimate single mind (the ultimate samadhi). Therefore the sutra says: “The three worthy ones and the ten sages dwell in the reward; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.” This ultimate single mind is the Tathagata’s Pure Land of Eternally Still Light. And the ultimate single mind is the Tathagata’s Dharmakaya as the treasury of the Dharma-realm. Apart from the Buddha alone, from the stage of Equal Enlightenment back to the first abiding, the forty-one stages of Dharmakaya great beings all partially break ignorance and partially verify real mark. Like a solar eclipse gradually becoming perfectly manifest and gradually recovering its light, theirs is only called the partially verified single mind (the partial-verification samadhi). For the solitary realizers and hearers, though the coarse delusions of view and thought are cut off, subtle ignorance remains entire. Like a solar eclipse where the round disc appears but the true body is not clear, theirs is only called the similar single mind (the similar samadhi). The patriarchs of successive generations, apart from those of partial verification and similarity, though greatly and thoroughly awakened and having greatly opened the perfect understanding, have not cut off the coarse delusions of view and thought. Like a solar eclipse covered by thin clouds, where one senses the sun but its round disc does not appear, theirs is only called the single mind of name (the samadhi of name). Therefore Master Ouyi said: “The right Dharma-eye within the stage of name — I do not know to whom it is entrusted today.” If one can rely on this single mind and diligently cultivate contemplation and practice, understanding that all the dependent and proper, form and mind, in the ten directions — whether form or void, whether defiled or pure — all return alike to the one true mind, sealed by one seal, without duality or difference, and can even perfectly suppress the afflictions of view and thought so that they no longer arise, then, like a solar eclipse where the thin clouds have stopped, though not wholly gone, never arising again, it may be called the single mind of contemplation and practice (the contemplation-practice samadhi). In former days Master Zhiyi manifested ascent to the fifth grade: that is this stage. We ordinary beings, though each inherently possesses it, have unfortunately never awakened. Like a solar eclipse covered by thick clouds, whose shadow does not appear; or like one blind with eye-disease who has never seen the sun and knows nothing at all, ours is only called the single mind of inherent principle (the samadhi of principle-nature). Of the six kinds of single mind described above, the first three belong to the sage stages. If one does not recite the Buddha and seek birth in the Land of Bliss, relying on the Buddha’s guidance to transcend the three realms horizontally and, once born in that land, join the stream of the sages, then one must by one’s own power know the mind and reach the source, cut off delusion and realize the truth, and transcend the three realms vertically before entering the sage stages. Who among the ordinary beings of the final age could do that?

Happily, our Shakyamuni World-Honored One, in the ocean of nirvana three thousand years ago, foreknew and foresaw. In compassion he thought of us ordinary beings of the final age, heavily hindered, shallow in faculty, our knowledge benighted, like the eye-diseased blind who can hardly see sun or sky: unable by our own power to know the mind and reach the source, cut off delusion and realize the truth, end birth and death, transcend the ordinary and enter the sage. We dwell always in the Saha world’s six paths of rebirth, enduring all afflictions, unable to escape. The Tathagata, wishing to pour out his original heart, therefore, without being asked, spoke of himself, and especially opened the Pure Land gate of borrowing the fruit to cultivate the cause, of relying on the Buddha for rebirth. He universally enables us beings who recite the Buddha: we need only give rise to faith, make vows, keep sincerity in the mind thought after thought, and hold Amitabha Buddha’s name, and we naturally and gradually accord with the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness and dwell at ease in the Tathagata’s real-mark right samadhi — like a river entering the sea, gradually entering, gradually deepening. Having entered the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness and dwelling at ease in the Tathagata’s real-mark right samadhi, one then knows that the name is the provisional aspect of the Tathagata’s fruit-awareness, and the fruit-awareness is the real aspect of the Tathagata’s name. One further knows that the Tathagata’s name was brought to perfection by the power of vows made in former lives. The Tathagata, from the real establishing the provisional, universally enables beings of the ten directions, by means of this provisional name, to hold it without forgetting thought after thought, and gradually to accord with the real, the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness. Having entered the real, the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness, one feels of oneself, while reciting the Buddha, that every phrase of the Buddha-name flows out from the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, and again one feels that every phrase of the Buddha-name returns into the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, fused and perfect, filling the Dharma-realm. This is what is meant by the Tathagata’s great name is the fruit-awareness, and the fruit-awareness is the Tathagata’s great name.

If all of us can comprehend as above and cultivate as above, then in the work of pure karma, though we have not yet cut off delusion and personally verified the single mind, we have at least entered the gate of the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real single mind. When we set to work, we feel we have a home to return to, a reliance, a sovereignty, a taste of the Dharma. No longer are we as before, like a restless monkey that has lost its training, drifting everywhere, seeking only filthy food, greedily chasing the six dusts, with no way to be gathered in. From now on, adding further diligence, we naturally make daily progress. If only we do not retreat to the end of life but perfume and cultivate according to the Dharma, then though we cannot personally verify it now, at the end of life the cause will still be strong. Why? Because the Tathagata’s real-mark fruit-awareness is vast and perfect, containing all the space of the ten directions. While we are rightly reciting the Buddha, we need only, at the place where each of us stirs and moves the mind, plant our feet firm, tread solid ground, and observe with mindfulness thought after thought, not letting it drift; and if we feel it drifting, gather it and make it return. If we can thus hold the name and thus observe thought after thought, it is called entering the Buddha’s fruit-awareness thought after thought and dwelling in the Buddha’s right samadhi mind after mind. Only take it up directly, without raising doubt and without giving rise to discrimination, and we naturally enter deep, gradually, into the Tathagata’s inconceivable realm. Therefore the ancients said: “When your body is in the Hanyuan Palace, why ask where Chang’an is?” Know that the Tathagata’s true fruit-awareness is one’s own pure original awakening, and one’s own pure original awakening is the Tathagata’s true fruit-awareness. This is what is meant by cause is fruit, cause and fruit simultaneous, direct and plain, the whole perfectly complete. Therefore the ancients said: “A single phrase of Amitabha is absolute and perfectly fused, beyond emotion and apart from views, unattainable and inconceivable.”

Indeed, though our consciousness differs from the Tathagata’s, our awakened nature is originally without distinction. Like a bubble entering water, it accords by nature. If one can plant one’s feet firm at a single thought and put down the whole body, then in that instant one enters the Buddha’s fruit-awareness and dwells in the Buddha’s right samadhi; from then on one may well recite the Buddha at peace, awaiting the Buddha’s welcome. Again, like a beggar who gains entry into a ruined temple: though it is not his own, he may borrow it to dwell in peace — far better than the open air of former days. Even if he moves about and wanders, he is fortunate enough to know when he leaves and when he returns. We practitioners of Buddha-recitation are likewise: we borrow the Tathagata’s bodhi fruit-awareness as our own bodhi cause-mind. Happily, by our Buddha’s compassion and his vows of former lives, we are enabled to take the name as our gate of entry, to be gathered home to the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness, and to dwell at ease in the Tathagata’s real-mark right samadhi. Though there be drifting and wandering, at a single moment of awareness we return. From then on we may also constantly borrow the pure water-ocean of the Tathagata’s real mark and bathe the whole body, at once feeling body and mind joyful and cool within and without. And we may borrow the fragrance and light of the Tathagata’s merit and wisdom to perfume and shine through the whole body, at once feeling body and mind at peace and transparent within and without. This is precisely what is meant by adorning oneself with the Buddha’s adornment and upholding oneself with the Buddha’s upholding. We wait only until the Saha seal is broken and the Pure Land scroll is complete, when the Buddha comes to receive and guide us to rebirth in the Land of Bliss. Then we may draw near the compassionate Father and study all Dharma-gates, fulfilling this great causal matter of single-mindedness, undisturbed: perfecting the Buddha-fruit above and saving beings below. Since there is such an inconceivable, supremely wondrous benefit, one should share the good with others — this alone accords with the great bodhi way. Therefore I have set out its essentials to offer universally to companions of the ten directions. May all friends in purity who read this sutra take heed, observe, reflect with right mindfulness, perfume and cultivate according to the Dharma, and together obtain the excellent benefit: in the present, dwelling in the Saha world yet entering deep into the Buddha-fruit; at the end of life, reborn in the Land of Bliss and ascending high upon a jeweled lotus. And may this be passed on everywhere and handed down by everyone, so that the Buddha-recitation samadhi may long abide in the world and the orthodox Pure Land teaching never be replaced. Now, wishing to make it brief and easy to hold, and to gather in all the meanings of the whole text, I restate them in a verse:
Right mindfulness is like the noonday sun; in the vast void it dwells at ease, its nurture done.
Its rounded light embraces boundless space; distinct and clear, known only to oneself.
The six-character great name, recited on and on, is worth in every sound more than the mani stone.
When dusk draws near, the Buddha comes in grace, to lead us straight to the West’s seven-jeweled place.

The eight lines above are a simile, displaying the Buddha-recitation samadhi as perfect in fact and principle, complete in essence and function. They are what is called the power of cause and fruit according with each other, the power of concentration and wisdom perfectly clear, the power of self and other responding to each other, and the power of being and Buddha seeing each other. These four practices and four powers are each distinct; one who understands will see them and naturally be clear. If practitioners of Buddha-recitation are willing to read them until familiar and memorize them, then when reciting the Buddha they may contemplate the meaning along with the words; when long perfumed and matured, they naturally feel their body within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, dwelling at ease in right samadhi. If in ordinary times they are well practiced and can recite the Buddha within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, then at the end of life they will also see the Buddha within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind — as a mirror shows an image, as water captures a reflection, with no need for forcing, naturally and of itself. Companions in Buddha-recitation, please do not doubt it.

Note: the six kinds of single mind described in this piece accord with the teaching and display the stages of the Buddha-recitation samadhi, so as to avoid vagueness. Except for the first three single minds, which may be called attainment and verification, the latter three are only called borrowing the fruit to cultivate the cause, and may not be called attainment or verification. If one does not speak of attainment and verification, then by this perfuming and cultivation the benefit is immeasurable; but if one deliberately speaks falsely, saying one has attained and verified, one instead invites evil misfortune. Therefore the ancients spoke only of cultivation and holding, not of attainment and verification. Why? As to the Buddha-recitation samadhi, if we speak of taking it up and entering the gate, it is special compared with all Dharma-gates; if we speak of verifying the fruit, it is wholly the same as the teaching. Yet the matter of verifying the fruit was difficult even in ancient times: that is why Master Zhiyi manifested dwelling in contemplation and practice, and Master Ouyi manifested dwelling in the stage of name. Seen thus, even the ancients were so — who among the ordinary beings of the final age is more easily capable? Reading this, one may avoid confounding the ordinary with the sage and committing the offense of false speech. But if one is merely willing to bring forth the mind and cultivate, the merit is inconceivable: in the present eliminating karmic hindrances and greatly increasing merit and wisdom; at the end of life reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, ascending high upon a jeweled lotus. May all companions each know this, perfume and cultivate according to the Dharma, and return together to the Pure Land.
Appendix: The One-Practice Samadhi from the Manjushri Prajna Sutra

The Buddha said: “Good men and good women who wish to enter the one-practice samadhi should dwell in a quiet place, set aside all scattered thoughts, take no hold of appearances, and fix the mind on one Buddha, calling his name single-mindedly, turning the body squarely toward the direction where that Buddha is. If one can, with one Buddha, continue thought after thought, then within that mindfulness one can see the Buddhas of past, future, and present. Why? The merit of recollecting one Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, and is not two with the merit of all Buddhas. The inconceivable Buddha-Dharma is equal and without distinction: all ride upon the one suchness and accomplish supreme perfect enlightenment, all possessing immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence. One who thus enters the one-practice samadhi knows fully that the Dharma-realms of the Buddhas, countless as the sands of the Ganges, are without mark of difference.”

Explanation: the Buddha’s words “the Dharma-realm is without mark of difference” mean that the Tathagatas of the ten directions alike verify the suchness-Dharmakaya. The Lotus Sutra says: “The Tathagatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharmakaya.” And the Diamond Sutra says: “The Tathagata is the thusness of all dharmas.” This is what is meant by contemplating the body as real mark, and contemplating the Buddha and beings likewise. One who wishes to see Amitabha Buddha’s suchness-Dharmakaya sees it at will by this means. To enter this realm and dwell in this realm is called entering and dwelling in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is also called entering and dwelling in the Buddha’s right samadhi. Those who understand enter clearly; those who do not, enter darkly. If one is merely willing, thought after thought, to keep sincerity in the mind and hold Amitabha Buddha’s name, then even foolish men and women can be made to penetrate secretly the Buddha’s wisdom and accord darkly with the wonder of the Way. Why? Because the one true Dharma-realm is originally the common source of sages and ordinary beings, the one substance of beings and Buddhas. If one is willing to recite the Buddha sincerely, it can cause one gradually to turn from the dust and unite with awakening, to return from the false to the true — like a bubble entering water, according by nature. When the accord reaches its utmost, the whole body is complete and round. Hence it is said: all possessing immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence. Seeing this, one knows further that the Land of Ultimate Bliss, with its proper and dependent adornments, is wholly contained and gathered within it, sealed by one seal. Though we do not see it now, at the end of life we shall certainly see it. Our reciting the Buddha now is like digging a pond to await the moon: when the full moon is in the sky, it appears in the pond of itself. May everyone believe and accept; please do not doubt.
Author’s Postscript

I reflect with all my heart: the one true ocean of awakening is the perfect fusion of ten thousand virtues; sages and ordinary beings share one source, beings and Buddhas are one substance. Therefore the ancients said: “The afflictions that beings bring into activity are precisely the Buddhas’ true body of wisdom.” Truly these are wondrous words, clear and thorough to the utmost. Seen with the Buddha-eye, the beings of the nine realms are all within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, alike entering samadhi, alike accomplishing right enlightenment. The Tathagata’s true fruit-awareness is precisely the beings’ pure original awakening. Originally all are one mind, in the end without duality or difference. But because the Tathagata in former times on the cause-ground cultivated and verified through kalpas, perfect in merit and wisdom, filled with fragrance and light, complete in the adornments of the three bodies and four lands — the land is the body, the body is the land, body and land non-dual, real mark one suchness — he forever enjoys wondrous bliss, his benefit inexhaustible. Beings, since beginningless time, have through kalpas been benighted, their afflictions confused, their karmic consciousness obstructing them. Though they are within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, for kalpas like dust-motes they are unaware and unknowing. They do not see the Tathagata’s fruit-awareness real mark and do not receive the Tathagata’s benefit of fragrance and light. They dwell always in the six paths of rebirth, enduring all afflictions, and on into the future without ceasing. It is like the eye-diseased blind who have never seen sun or sky: though beneath the sun and sky, they receive no benefit of light, and always suffer the pain of darkness, inversion, and falling, to the end of life with no escape. Therefore our Shakyamuni World-Honored One, with great wisdom’s perfect contemplation and great compassion’s universal pity, within the Three-Vehicle teaching and among all Dharma-gates, especially opened the one gate of the Pure Land: borrowing the fruit to cultivate the cause, relying on the Buddha for rebirth. He teaches all we benighted beings of the Saha world in the final age, when we hear of the proper and dependent adornments of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: if we wish to seek birth in that land, we need only give rise to faith and vows and hold Amitabha Buddha’s name; long held and matured, we naturally gain single-mindedness, undisturbed. What is called single-mindedness, undisturbed, teaches us that while we are rightly reciting the Buddha, we dwell thought after thought within Amitabha Buddha’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind. Borrowing the containing, nurturing, upholding, and fusing power of Amitabha Buddha’s perfect fruit-awareness real wondrous mind, mind and mind fuse: like water resting in water, like water joining water, long and long becoming a piece, naturally undisturbed. Having become a piece and undisturbed, it is what is called one thought the whole, the whole one thought: one’s own mind melts into the Buddha’s mind, and the Buddha’s mind merges into one’s own. To see the Tathagata’s true fruit-awareness is to see one’s own pure original awakening. Therefore the sutra says: “When that person is about to die, Amitabha Buddha with all the sages appears before him.” Appears before him means it appears within the practitioner’s own pure original-awakening mind. Hence others do not see it; only the practitioner alone sees it. If the practitioner’s pure karma has long been accomplished, then the excellent scenes of the Pure Land may appear in samadhi or in dreams, and may be seen even in this life (in ancient times there were very many such); it is not that one must wait for the end of life to see them. It is like a clear pond when the full moon is in the sky: it appears of itself — no need to doubt. Again, Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta said: “Without other skillful means, one naturally opens the mind.” Without other skillful means, one naturally opens the mind means: without borrowing any other skillful means, one need only recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha, relying wholly on the fragrance and light of the Tathagata’s merit and wisdom to contain, nurture, uphold, and shine through the whole body; obtaining the Buddha’s atmosphere, one can cause affliction and karmic consciousness gradually to dissolve, and the mind-ground of real mark naturally to open. Having opened the mind-ground, one there and then enters deep into real mark, form and emptiness perfectly fused, thus and unmoved. Therefore the sutra says: “I, originally on the cause-ground, by the mind that recites the Buddha, entered the patience of non-arising.” Entering the patience of non-arising means entering the patience of real mark. To verify real mark personally is called attaining non-arising; having attained non-arising, one is complete in the power of patience. Indeed, the Tathagata’s real-mark fruit-awareness is originally vast and boundless, its measure equal to the Dharma-realm; it is called the Dharmakaya as the treasury of the Dharma-realm, containing all the space of the ten directions, embracing all beings of the nine realms, not one of whom is outside it. Therefore we, through countless kalpas, have always been within Amitabha Buddha’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, right up to this day, and have never departed from it. It is what is called originally not going out in the past, and now not entering. If one can deeply believe that one’s present single thought’s five-aggregate body and mind is always within Amitabha Buddha’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, originally neither going out nor coming in, and if the practitioner, while reciting the Buddha, thus observes thought after thought and so enters the Buddha’s fruit-awareness thought after thought and dwells in the Buddha’s right samadhi — then, able thus to enter the Buddha’s fruit-awareness and dwell in the Buddha’s right samadhi thought after thought, one does not seek single mind and yet is naturally single mind. Why? Because the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness is originally mind, Buddha, and beings — the three without difference. Buddha and beings share one true wondrous mind, without duality or difference. If we wish to seek single-mindedness, undisturbed, we should take the Buddha-fruit as our home and our guiding principle. Apart from the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness, where else is there a single-mindedness, undisturbed? Now we see many practitioners who wish to seek single-mindedness, undisturbed, yet do not know the road of mind-nature and do not understand the guiding principle of home. They only know to strive anxiously, using self-power alone to suppress deluded thoughts, hoping to gain single mind quickly. Because this cannot fuse with the Buddha’s power, they often rush themselves into trouble. Even to the point of having no recourse, they say instead: “I have always heard that Buddha-recitation is secure — why does the Buddha not protect me?” Seen with the right eye, one cannot help but sigh. They do not know that the cause-mind of beings and the fruit-awareness of the Buddha are originally not separated by a hair. When the practitioner recites the Buddha, he need only put down the whole body, keep sincerity thought after thought, and hold the Buddha’s name — like water returning to water, like water joining water; long and long matured, unawares the true and the false accord, and naturally mind and Buddha are one suchness. At that time he feels only the ease and joy of body and mind — what trouble could there be? Therefore, not measuring my own mediocrity and folly, but only because my wish to benefit people is urgent, I have taken the two meanings of the smaller Amitabha Sutra and the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Buddha-Recitation by Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, and at the most essential points, in plain language, explained them clearly, briefly setting them out, smoothing the meaning, leading into the Buddha-fruit and dwelling in the Buddha’s right samadhi. For these two sutras belong especially to concentrated goodness. As for the causal mind of beings and the fruit-awareness of the Buddha, their bearing is immense, most intimate and most urgent. Yet though the five Pure Land sutras each expound the provisions for pure karma and supplement what practitioners lack, if we seek what accords with faculty and principle, what saves effort and is easy to cultivate, then only these two sutras are most suited to the faculties of practitioners in the final age. They rely wholly on the containing, nurturing, and upholding power of the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness, and on the power of one’s own sincere right mindfulness dwelling in the Buddha-fruit, fusing with each other. When the fusion reaches its utmost, pure karma becomes a piece. It is like crossing the sea by ship: once aboard the ferry of universal deliverance, the practitioner need only sit at ease and he naturally reaches the other shore. Practitioners of Buddha-recitation are likewise: having entered the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness, they need only recite the Buddha with a settled mind and they naturally reach the other shore of the Land of Bliss. I do not presume to hold to one and discard the rest; I take what accords with faculty and principle, what saves effort and is easy to cultivate. The other Pure Land sutras and treatises I do not fail to read, nor do I fail to cultivate all the merits of scattered goodness. But according to one’s strength and station: if one has the ability to do them, it is beauty added to beauty and goodness added to goodness. If one is poor and lacking, without the power to do them, then with this merit of concentrated goodness one may still be reborn. But if one has neither concentrated nor scattered goodness, rebirth in the West is difficult. That is why, among people today, seven out of ten find rebirth difficult: all because they lack the power of concentrated goodness, relying only on the merit of scattered goodness, faith, vows, and dedication. Even if they are reborn, it is mostly by strain. The practitioners of old had deep and thick faculties: apart from scattered goodness, whether they cultivated contemplation or held the name, all could attain concentration. Therefore a thousand were reborn out of a thousand, a hundred out of a hundred. If they were not reborn, then nothing; but if reborn, their auspicious signs were manifest and they departed at will. Practitioners of today have shallow and thin faculties: with a settled mind cultivating contemplation, nine out of ten find it difficult. Only these two practices, together with the Pure Land repentance rites, are within the reach of both wise and foolish, from the shallow into the deep, gradually gaining excellent benefit. But one must put down the whole body, keep sincerity thought after thought, recite the Buddha and bow to the Buddha, and perfume and cultivate long; then suddenly one feels one’s own body as if in space, utterly without hindrance. At that time one has already accorded with the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness and dwells within the Tathagata’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind. And again, like a kernel of fruit dwelling within the fruit, self-power and other-power suddenly feel intimate, within and without one suchness, neither going out nor coming in. If one can thus perfume and cultivate to the utmost, one feels still more the transparency within and without and the fusion of the whole body. This is what is meant by one mind, ten thousand dharmas; ten thousand dharmas, one mind. Sages and ordinary beings share one source, beings and Buddhas one substance. One morning, when the Saha seal is broken and the Pure Land scroll is complete, the excellent scenes of the West seem to be right before one’s eyes; by the Buddha’s spiritual power, in the snap of a finger one arrives. Then one knows that though the Land of Bliss is distant, it is originally within the great chamber of fragrance and light of Amitabha Buddha’s perfect fruit-awareness, not a hair’s breadth away. If those who read this book always comprehend it thus and cultivate thus, they may be said to enter well into the Tathagata’s chamber of fragrance and light. And if Upasaka Huijue publishes this book, his joy fulfilling his vow, then this foolish sincerity of mine, my humble hope, will also be satisfied.

Postscript by Liaoran, the gruel-and-rice monk boarding at Lingyan, on the first day of the third month of the thirty-fifth year of the Republic of China, at the Non-Retreat Hermitage of the Fohai Quanzhen Peach Orchard.

Appendix: Master Hanshan’s Inscription on the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi. Recite the Buddha, recite the mind; recite the mind, recite the Buddha. The Buddha is not outside the mind; the mind is not a thing. The light of self-nature — mind after mind illuminates and shines. Deluded thoughts hide their traces; the body is an empty valley. The Pure Land never leaves the present; lotus flowers always cushion both feet. Why wait for death to be born there? Right now, neither going out nor coming in. This is precisely the universal-light samadhi; it lies only in a single shout of the person at hand. Explanation: mind, Buddha, and beings — the three are without difference, one and the same true suchness real mark; it is precisely within this that one may settle the mind and recite the Buddha. So it may be said: every phrase of the Buddha-name flows out from the light of self-nature, illuminating and understanding all dharmas as originally void and still. Deluded thoughts naturally hide their traces; the body is likewise like an empty valley. There is only one phrase of the Buddha-name, clear and distinct, like a dripping spring, continuing without break. Though the body dwells in the Saha world, it is as if in the Pure Land: thought after thought dwelling at ease within Amitabha’s perfect fruit-awareness real mind, neither going out nor coming in. This is precisely the universal-light samadhi, gathering in all Amitabha’s three bodies and four lands, all encompassed within it. One morning, when Saha conditions end and Pure Land conditions ripen, the excellent scenes of the Land of Bliss appear before one’s eyes. This is what is meant by reborn, then certainly reborn; gone, yet in truth not gone.
Appendix: A Record of the Rebirth of Madam Jiang, Mother of the Yuan Family

At Lingyan Mountain I met a certain Mrs. Chen, a native of Hubei. In recent years she had taken refuge with the venerable Master Miao of this temple; she now lives in Shanghai, and because she finds the household noisy and crowded, a hindrance to cultivation, she often comes to the mountain to dwell quietly and recite the Buddha. One day she heard me say that the merit of Buddha-recitation is inconceivable: many foolish men and women who cannot read a single character, of whom in ordinary times one sees only that they can recite the Buddha and nothing else, at the end of life reveal all that they can do, while many who in ordinary times are able to write and speak cannot match them at the end. On this reasoning, could it be that Amitabha Buddha’s love is partial? It is only that foolish men and women can, thought after thought, die to the mind, tread solid ground step by step, and focus on a single gate. Like a dragon entering the sea, gradually entering, gradually deepening, they obtain the Buddha’s atmosphere and naturally can do what they could not. Understanding this principle, one may well recite the Buddha. When she had heard this, the next day she brought four photographs and said to me: “These are portraits of my adoptive mother, old Mrs. Yuan. The first was taken when my mother was in good health, reciting the Buddha. The second was taken when my mother showed illness in bed. The third was taken when my mother was about to return to the West, foreknowing the time, bathing and changing clothes, shaving her head and receiving the precepts, and then lying on her right side. The fourth was taken when my mother, at the end of life, sat upright in majesty, called the Buddha’s name aloud, saw the Buddha come to welcome her, and quietly passed into quiescence. Yesterday, when I heard the Master say that the merit of Buddha-recitation is inconceivable, it matched exactly the many facts about my mother. So I have brought these photographs today to report to you and ask the Master to bear witness.” She then respectfully set out before me the various facts of my mother’s life and death, briefly as follows. My adoptive mother was Madam Jiang of the Yuan family, Dharma name Changjing, her home in Hankou, Hubei. She sought refuge under Master Qingde and received the five precepts at Yuanzhao Temple in Hankou. She kept a long-term vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha for thirty-three years, and was reborn in the West at the age of sixty-nine. In ordinary times she was diligent in cultivation, never slackening in cold or heat. Every morning she rose at four o’clock to recite the Buddha, and by day she constantly bowed to the Buddha. Even in the hottest days, when her clothes were soaked with sweat, she would change into several haiqing robes. Thus was my mother’s ordinary diligence in cultivation. If she saw a suffering person with no clothes coming to the door to beg, she would rather take off the clothes she herself was wearing and give them away. Or if she met a poor person who had no way to pass the New Year and had come to steal from her house, she would let the thief take the things, and at the same time fill a bowl from the kitchen and let the thief eat his fill before leaving. Thus was my mother’s ordinary giving to the hungry and poor. Once, when a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks was held at Guiyuan Temple, about a thousand people came to receive the offering. She heard that what had been prepared in the pot was not enough to feed them, that the vegetables in the market had long been sold out, and that there was no way to prepare more. My mother said: “Please add three more loads of water to the pot.” Afterwards, when the crowd ate it, the flavor was excellent and fresh. Thus was my mother’s ordinary offering to the Sangha. In the first month of the thirty-third year of the Republic, my mother showed a slight illness. Once she wept and said: “Hankou will meet with a great disaster.” The family asked her: “Shall we be afraid?” My mother said: “We are not in much danger, but the people’s suffering will be unbearable.” After the tenth of the fourth month, as she was about to return to the West, she saw with her own eyes the Three Sages of the West come to welcome her, and she knew the hour of her return had come. She instructed: “Go quickly to the Buddha hall and burn incense; the Buddha has come to welcome me — I am going.” The family said: “Old Mother, since you are returning to the West, you should ask Amitabha Buddha to choose a good date. Today is an ordinary day; there is no need to go.” My mother said: “I know.” Some days later my mother said: “You have harmed me; these past days Amitabha Buddha has not come.” The family said: “Old Mother, do not be anxious; when the hour of your return to the West arrives, the Buddha will surely come again to welcome you.” The next day my mother said: “I wish to sit in a jar; the jar must be lined with rush pith and rosin. Hurry and have it all prepared for me.” At that time it happened that the Japanese soldiers were causing turmoil and all trades were on strike; in the market there was only one jar, and that a poor one. Though it had been bought, it had not yet been carried home. My mother said: “Hurry and bring the jar.” The family said: “The jar has not arrived.” My mother said: “Why did you buy me this poor jar?” A little later the various things all arrived, and the family looked: it was indeed a poor one. My mother said again: “Why did you buy me this broken rush pith?” The family said: “It is one whole bundle.” My mother said: “If you do not believe it, open it and see.” The family opened it, and it was indeed broken. Thus did my mother’s mind, as her end drew near, perceive things. On the morning of the seventeenth my mother said: “I wish to shave my head. Go quickly to Guiyuan Temple and ask the chief seat monk to come and give me the precepts.” She said also: “Quickly burn sandalwood water and bathe me.” When the bathing and changing of clothes were finished, the chief seat monk arrived, shaved my mother’s head, and conferred the novice precepts. After receiving the precepts, my mother lay on her right side. Thus did my mother, as her end drew near, revere the precepts and Vinaya. On the morning of the twentieth my mother said: “Today I am going to return to the West. Go quickly to Guiyuan Temple and ask the chief seat monk to bring the monks to help me return to the West.” By eight o’clock the chief seat monk and the monks arrived; my mother asked to be helped to sit upright in a chair, her feet crossed in the lotus posture, the precept certificate hung on her breast, a recitation rosary in her hand. My mother said: “Bring a cloth pillow to put behind my back.” Again, because the crowd blocked the way, my mother’s face showed anxiety. The crowd said: “We will make way in the middle.” My mother said joyfully: “Amitabha Buddha with all the sages has long since arrived. Do not weep; recite the Buddha with me.” Having said this, she herself called the Buddha’s name several times, and the crowd recited the Buddha’s name together. By ten o’clock my mother quietly passed into quiescence, as if entering Chan concentration. Thus did my mother peacefully return to the West at the last. The next day at ten o’clock, when she was placed in the jar, she was upright as before. On the day of cremation, those who followed the funeral and recited the Buddha numbered about a thousand, and all sighed that it was rare. When the relics were gathered, the bones had a golden hue and there were pale white sharira, seven in all, large and small. Most rare of all: when my mother was placed in the jar she wore a gray haiqing robe, and after cremation four corners of the haiqing were picked out, turned blue in color, with rows of bead-like threads along the edges, snow-white and distinct, and when two people pulled at them with both hands they would not break. In the winter of the thirty-third year, when the national army was about to recover the city, Hankou was indeed bombed everywhere and the people’s houses were nearly all destroyed, yet my mother’s house alone was safe and unharmed. Recalling my mother’s prophecy, there was not the least discrepancy. Just as the bombing was happening, someone saw three bombs fall on my mother’s house and clapped his hands, sighing: “What a pity — Mrs. Chen was such a good person, and now she too is finished.” Later, on inquiry, it turned out that the bombs had fallen separately on the neighboring houses. All who knew sighed: “It was all moved by old Mrs. Yuan’s past practice and added to by the Buddha’s power.” Thus did my mother’s spiritual influence protect after her death. Hearing it, I could not but deeply admire. I respectfully note: that Madam Yuan obtained seven white sharira after death indicates that in life her precepts were pure and her resolve in the Way firm. That after cremation four corners of the haiqing remained undestroyed indicates that in life she was diligent in practice and cultivated assiduously. That in her illness she knew clearly, without having seen with her own eyes, about the earthen jar and the rush pith is proof enough that her mind was like clear water, in which all things appear. That in former days the added water made the feast delicious and fresh was brought about by her sincere mind and accomplished by her vow-power. That at the end she shaved her head and devoutly received the novice precepts accords exactly with the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations and its middle-grade upper birth and middle-grade middle birth. Judging by these various auspicious signs, in the Dharma-ending age they may be called rare. Moreover, at a time when the situation was in confusion, people’s minds anxious and fearful, to be able at the end of life still to sit upright and recite the Buddha, see the Buddha come to welcome her, and return peacefully to the West — this is rarer still than rare. Those who style themselves wise and mock foolish people for reciting the Buddha — seeing this, should they not die of shame? I am not by nature a literary man, and I never record biographies for others; nor did Mrs. Chen intentionally ask me to record this. But seeing that the photographs provide solid evidence, exactly matching the facts Mrs. Chen related, allowing no room for the slightest speculation, one cannot help but be moved and filled with admiration. Compared with the many who speak falsely and ornament their accounts, the distance is as heaven from an abyss. Moreover, Mrs. Chen often came to the mountain to recite the Buddha, staying several months at a time, and everyone knew her resolve in the Way to be genuine and her words free of falsehood. Even these various facts she had never told anyone; but because she heard what I said the other day and it exactly matched the facts about her mother, her heart was moved and she came especially to tell me. I reflected that the cause of her coming was strange and rare, and must surely be the unseen addition of old Mrs. Yuan and the working of her power in the Way, borrowing the convergence of conditions to make this record of rebirth. Therefore I take up my pen and respectfully record the various facts related by Mrs. Chen, and together with the photograph of Madam Yuan reciting the Buddha and passing away seated at the end of life, publish them in the Honghua Monthly to share with fellow cultivators, so that those who see and hear may make of it an augmentative condition. May all companions who read this record take heed, observe, and deeply attend to it.

Respectfully recorded by Liaoran, the gruel-and-rice monk boarding at Lingyan, on the day of Shakyamuni World-Honored One’s attainment of the Way, in the twelfth month of the thirty-sixth year of the Republic of China, at the Non-Retreat Hermitage of the Fohai Quanzhen Peach Orchard.
Appendix: A Verse on the Merit of Revering the Sharira
All companions, revere the sharira — through a hundred thousand kalpas hard to meet. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, in great compassion, send down the five hues.
True sharira, granted to our sight, opens the mind-ground, far removes the dust of toil, brings us into the Buddha’s wisdom. If with reverence, bow the body down.
Praise with the mouth, rejoice in the heart, karma-hindrances dissolve, merit and wisdom grow. This fruit and reward only the Buddha knows. If you recite the Buddha,
ever recollect in the mind, turn the karmic consciousness, accomplish the Buddha’s wisdom, move the Buddha to welcome you, arrive at the lotus pond, the lotus opens, ascend the grades.
Pure wondrous bliss, hard to conceive; learn from the Buddha, never parted; patience attained, wielding compassion and wisdom, save all beings.
Together return to the West, merit and wisdom perfected, realize bodhi. Revering the sharira benefits thus. May all companions deeply attend.
Appendix: Ten Songs of the Peace and Bliss of the West
To all companions I say: recite the Buddha name; aloud or silently, the merit is the same.
Recite with all your heart, with single earnest mind, and from the dust you turn, to waking truth inclined.
Let go the four great elements, hold nothing tight; within the true mind settle, there to rest aright.
Its wonder, deep as sea, no words can hold: this is Amitabha’s great awakening, perfect and untold.
Keep the right mindfulness, and stay awake and clear; let no dull torpor come, no random wandering near.
Thought after thought within the true mind rest, and death will surely bring the Land of Bliss at last.
Invite the Buddha’s welcome, leave the fivefold dust; in the seven-jeweled pond a lotus holds you fast.
When the lotus opens, join the sages’ stream; with all the ocean host learn near the Buddha’s gleam.
Ground of gold and towers of seven-jeweled light, kalavinka birds and peacocks bright.
Rows of jeweled trees stand adorned and fair, flowers and fruits ablaze with radiance everywhere.
Rare fragrance breathed, celestial music heard; in the sky the jeweled net hangs thick with bells.
The gentle breeze sets all to chiming ring, and in true bliss we quite forget everything.
Drink sweet ambrosia, sip the cream and curd; at mealtimes comes the seven-jeweled bowl — no word.
A hundred rare flavors, tasted as you please; no need of cleansing, no impurity, no disease.
The seven-jeweled pond, how wide it lies, where gods and humans bathe beneath the skies.
Warm, cold, shallow, deep, as each one wills; its floor of golden sand no dust can soil.
If you would travel far, take the spirit-feet; at will the Buddhas of the ten directions greet.
Flying crosswise, in freedom without bound, in but a moment all ten trillion lands are found.
Realize the Dharmakaya, vast and wide; all lands of the ten directions are held inside.
In countless bodies sit at many a bodhi seat, saving all beings, perfect enlightenment complete.
Appendix: A Letter from Upasaka Tang Yougang

To my revered teacher Liaoran, in kind regard. I bow and write with respect: whenever I read your great work Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light, I never fail to stroke the volume and sigh long. For the scholars of this world, with their power to sweep away clouds and mist, their diligence that bears darkness and chases the dawn, their daily advance and monthly store, their wisdom that exhausts all they have seen and heard, still linger at the mysterious and strange, or halt their tracks at the phantom city; I regret only that I cannot grasp the very clue of it and break their narrow views.

Your grandmotherly heart is earnest and far-reaching, broadly benefiting beings. You have shaken forth a rare, wondrous sound and produced an outstanding masterpiece. This vast and mighty writing is like strange flowers and rare herbs, filling the eyes with radiance. Thus its literary brilliance has but to issue forth, and it seems the Buddha-land is already accomplished; again, like a jeweled flower first opening, its rare fragrance is heard throughout the ten directions. Therefore the whole world vies to see it, the gods lean down to listen, the great sages send down auspicious signs, and sharira fall in profusion. When it first appeared, it was like the new crescent moon, enough to break the deep darkness of the long night. Now that it circulates in the world, it is like the bright sun at midday, shedding further light over the thousand worlds. One suspects that an ancient worthy has come again, continuing the lamp of wisdom today. Wherever it goes on the southern continent, the Brahma sound is heard everywhere; one imagines that in the ponds of the Western land lotuses are racing to bloom. I rejoice that wise and foolish alike may hold it, and sigh that the clear and the dim receive it equally. Its perfect light shines everywhere, its body as lustrous as the bright moon; the fragrance of its nature perfumes all, its mind exceeding the measure of the vast void. Gang, who am still on the ground of learning and have fortunately not yet left my seat, now reads your great writing and my heart is freely opened. My knowledge is like fire kindled, ready to burn the forest of afflictions; my wisdom is like a prairie blaze, suddenly awakening me at the shout before my face. If in days to come there be the condition, then beneath the Diamond Seat I shall surely come to bow before you. If my spirit can be taught, then in the land of white snow I respectfully beg you to settle my mind-source. With this I respectfully submit, awaiting your jade voice. May you be healthy, joyful, peaceful, and auspicious. With utmost reverence, unsurpassed.
In the thirty-sixth year of the Republic, at the season of Cold Dew. The disciple Tang Yougang prostrates himself to the ground and sets this forth.
